rationale: In this app's BSB, three of Micah 7:6's four clauses reappear in Matthew 10:35-36. One is identical ("a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law"), and two match in all their key words ("a daughter" ... "against her mother"; "A man’s enemies" ... "the members of his own household"), the only differences being Micah's "rises", which Matthew lacks, and Micah's "are" where Matthew has "will be". The first clause differs: Micah has "a son dishonors his father", Matthew "a man against his father", and Matthew frames the whole with "For I have come to turn". The BSB itself prints 10:35-36 inside quotation marks, and the Pulpit Commentary says Jesus "adopts Micah's (Micah 7:6) description". Matthew gives no citation formula, which is why the type is allusion rather than quotation (as with Psalm 37:11 in Matthew 5:5); the sustained match, three of four clauses, one identical, and the BSB's own quotation marks, is why the label is strong. Commentators read on Biblehub describe the borrowing at different strengths: Barnes, "taken from Micah 7:6"; Expositor's Greek Testament, "reproduces freely"; Meyer, "Involuntary recollection"; and the Pulpit Commentary notes that "The wording is hardly taken from the LXX" (in the Greek, Matthew has kata where the Septuagint has epi, and the Septuagint's last clause adds pantes, "all").
